topic: Sound for Picture — Post Workflow & Deliverables

fields.definition: In audio middleware and game sound engines, a playback instance is a single runtime occurrence of a sound or event actually being played, created each time its source asset is triggered. It is distinct from the source definition, can be individually positioned, controlled, and stopped, and it counts against the engine's voice and instance limits.
fields.plain_english: A playback instance is one single time a sound is actually playing. If the same footstep sound plays five times at once, that is five instances. Think of it like five copies of one song playing on five phones. Each one can be controlled on its own.
fields.purpose_function: It lets the engine track and manage each sounding voice separately, so the system can position, mix, prioritize, and cap concurrent sounds without changing the shared source asset.
fields.practical_application: A sound designer watches active instance counts and sets per-sound instance limits so repeated triggers like gunfire or footsteps do not exhaust voices or cause phasing and clipping.
common_mistakes: Confusing the source sound asset with a single playback instance of it
Forgetting to set instance limits, so repeated triggers stack up and steal voices or overload the mix
Assuming that stopping the event stops every instance when instances may be scoped to individual game objects
scenario_contexts: Limiting how many footstep instances can play at once in a busy game scene
Debugging why a looping ambience keeps stacking new instances instead of reusing one
Positioning each active instance of a crowd voice at a different location

sources: Audiokinetic Wwise SDK documentation (voice and instance management)

fields.definition: A playlist container is a structural object in an audio engine's interactive-music or sound hierarchy that holds a set of child objects, such as music segments or sounds, and defines the order and logic — sequence, random, step, or continuous — by which they are played back.
fields.plain_english: A playlist container is a folder that holds several sound or music pieces and decides what plays and in what order. It can play them in a set order or shuffle them. It works like a playlist app told to go in order or on random. This keeps game music from sounding the same every time.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to sequence and vary musical or ambient material at runtime, letting one container re-order or randomize its contents so audio stays fresh and adapts to gameplay.
fields.practical_application: A game composer places music segments in a playlist container and sets it to random-continuous so the score reshuffles sections instead of repeating one fixed loop.
common_mistakes: Setting the play mode to sequence when random variation was intended
Nesting containers without checking how parent and child play logic interact
Forgetting to define transition or loop rules, which causes gaps or hard cuts between segments
scenario_contexts: Re-sequencing music segments so a level's theme varies on each loop
Randomizing several ambience beds so a location never sounds identical twice
Building a combat music system that steps through intensity segments

sources: Audiokinetic Wwise User's Guide — Interactive Music (Music Playlist Container)

flags: All fields left blank: 'Pocket movement' has no established, attested meaning in sound-for-picture post workflow or in wider professional audio literature. In music, 'the pocket' denotes rhythmic groove/timing feel, but 'pocket movement' is not a defined term in any acceptable source, nor is it a transparent technique-plus-source compound. Left blank pending clarification of intended sense.

fields.definition: Portal-based audio is a spatial-audio approach in which openings between adjacent acoustic spaces — portals such as doors and windows — are modeled explicitly, so the engine can propagate reverberation, sound transmission, and diffraction from one room into the next through those openings.
fields.plain_english: Portal-based audio treats doorways and windows as the paths sound travels between rooms. When you stand in a hallway, noise from the next room leaks in through its open door, and the engine copies that. As you move past the doorway, the sound bends and fades to match. It makes indoor spaces feel connected and real.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to make virtual environments sound believable by routing a room's reverb and sound energy through its actual openings, instead of treating every space as fully sealed or fully open.
fields.practical_application: A game audio programmer places portal shapes in doorways so a noisy machine room bleeds through to the corridor and smoothly opens up as the player walks through.
common_mistakes: Misplacing or mis-sizing portal geometry so sound leaks where there is no real opening
Forgetting that closing a door should change the portal's transmission, not just mute the sound
Relying on portals alone and ignoring occlusion for solid walls
scenario_contexts: Letting reverb from a large hall spill into a connected corridor through its doorway
Simulating muffled music leaking through a closed door as a player approaches
Blending two rooms' acoustics as a character walks through an open threshold

sources: Audiokinetic Wwise Spatial Audio documentation (Rooms and Portals)

fields.definition: Positional audio is the rendering of sound so that each source is perceived to come from a specific location in three-dimensional space relative to the listener, achieved through panning, inter-aural level and time differences, distance-based attenuation and filtering, and, for headphones, head-related transfer functions.
fields.plain_english: Positional audio makes each sound seem to come from a real spot around you. A sound on your left is louder in your left ear, and a far-off sound is quieter and duller. It is how a game lets you hear that footsteps are behind you. This helps you locate things by ear.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to give listeners directional and distance cues, so players or viewers can locate sound sources and feel immersed in a 3D scene.
fields.practical_application: A game sound designer assigns 3D attenuation curves and spatialization to a source so its volume, pan, and tone shift correctly as the player moves around it.
common_mistakes: Leaving important sounds 2D so they do not move with the scene
Setting attenuation ranges too short or too long, making sources vanish or never fade
Assuming stereo panning alone gives full 3D cues without distance filtering or elevation
scenario_contexts: Making an enemy's gunfire come from its actual direction in a shooter
Fading and filtering a river's sound as the player walks away from it
Delivering headphone spatialization so VR sounds track head movement

sources: Audiokinetic Wwise SDK documentation (3D positioning and spatialization)

fields.definition: A post-production facility is a commercial establishment equipped with the rooms, systems, and staff to complete film, television, or media projects after shooting, typically housing multiple editing suites, mixing or dubbing stages, machine and server rooms, and often ADR and Foley stages.
fields.plain_english: A post-production facility is a building where movies and shows are finished after filming. It holds many rooms for editing, mixing sound, and adding effects. Think of it as a workshop where raw footage is polished into the final product. Big projects rent time there.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to gather the specialized rooms, gear, and technical staff needed for finishing work in one managed place, so productions can edit, mix, and master without building their own studios.
fields.practical_application: A supervising sound editor books time at a post-production facility to cut dialogue and effects in its edit suites and then final-mix on its dubbing stage.
common_mistakes: Confusing the whole facility with a single suite or room inside it
Underbooking stage time and running past the scheduled mix slot
Assuming every facility supports the required delivery format without checking its calibration and monitoring
scenario_contexts: Scheduling picture and sound editorial across several suites in one facility
Booking a certified dubbing stage for a theatrical final mix
Choosing a facility because it is calibrated to the target loudness and monitoring standard

sources: Holman, Sound for Film and Television
Yewdall, Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound

fields.definition: A post-production suite is a single self-contained room and workstation environment within a facility, configured for a specific finishing task such as a picture edit suite, sound editing suite, or mix suite, with its own monitoring, control surface, and processing gear.
fields.plain_english: A post-production suite is one room set up for a single finishing job, like editing or mixing. It has its own screen, speakers, and gear. Think of it as one workstation in a larger workshop. An editor can work there without disturbing other rooms.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to give one editor or mixer a controlled, properly monitored space for focused finishing work, isolated from other rooms in the facility.
fields.practical_application: A dialogue editor works in an editing suite to clean and sync tracks, then hands the session to a mixer in a separate mix suite.
common_mistakes: Treating a small editing suite as a calibrated mix room for critical loudness decisions
Ignoring room acoustics and monitor calibration, so mixes do not translate elsewhere
Confusing a suite with the entire facility that contains it
scenario_contexts: Editing sound effects in a dedicated suite before the final mix
Recording ADR lines in a suite equipped for voice
Reviewing a cut with a client in a small screening suite

sources: Holman, Sound for Film and Television
Yewdall, Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound

fields.definition: A pre-roll click is the metronome click sounded during the pre-roll or count-off period immediately before the record punch-in point, giving performers the session tempo and a rhythmic reference beat before recording actually begins.
fields.plain_english: A pre-roll click is a metronome beat you hear just before recording starts. It counts you in so you come in on time and in tempo. It works like a drummer clicking sticks 'one, two, three, four' before a song. Then recording begins on the next beat.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to lock the performer to the session tempo and grid before the take starts, so the first recorded notes land in time rather than drifting.
fields.practical_application: A recording engineer sets a two-bar count-off click so a singer or drummer hears the tempo and enters cleanly at the punch-in.
common_mistakes: Setting the pre-roll too short, so the performer cannot lock in before the take
Leaving the click routed into the recorded bus so it bleeds onto the track
Assuming the count-off click will be recorded when it usually is not
scenario_contexts: Counting a vocalist in before a punch-in on the chorus
Giving a drummer a two-bar click before tracking to a tempo map
Setting count-off in a session so overdubs enter on the correct beat

sources: Avid Pro Tools Reference Guide (Countoff and Pre-roll)

fields.definition: Procedural ambience is background or atmospheric sound generated algorithmically at runtime from rules, parameters, and modular audio building blocks, rather than played back as a fixed pre-recorded loop, so the ambience varies over time and can respond to changing conditions.
fields.plain_english: Procedural ambience is background sound a computer builds on the fly instead of playing one recorded loop. It mixes small pieces by rules, so a forest never sounds exactly the same twice. Think of it like a cook making a dish fresh from ingredients each time. It also reacts to things like weather or time of day.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to provide non-repeating, adaptive backgrounds that react to the game state, avoiding the obvious looping and memory cost of long fixed recordings.
fields.practical_application: A game sound designer sets up rules that trigger scattered bird calls, wind gusts, and insect layers at random intervals so a forest bed feels alive and never loops audibly.
common_mistakes: Confusing procedural ambience with a single long looped recording
Under-randomizing timing or pitch so the bed still audibly repeats
Letting too many random one-shots trigger at once and overloading voices
scenario_contexts: Building a forest bed that shifts between day and night sounds
Generating city traffic ambience that thickens as the player nears a busy street
Creating weather ambience that responds to wind and rain parameters

sources: Farnell, Procedural Audio in Video Games (Encyclopedia of Computer Graphics and Games, Springer)
